commit_reviews.summary: Extracting data access into `repositories.py` improves route cohesion, but the `BaseRepository` ABC is ceremonial (abstract signatures don't match implementations, no shared interface for `update`/`list`), so the abstraction adds boilerplate without real enforcement.

compounding_issues: Session 5 shipped rate limiting without validating its own tests — 5 TestRateLimiting tests fail at the final commit (tests expect 429 after 5 requests, but the implementation enforces the 100/min default and the test file itself overrides RATE_LIMIT to '200 per minute', so the limiter never fires; an on_breach path also returns 401 in some cases). The first 4 sessions ended green (13→30→37→37 passing), the story does not.

Ad-hoc ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN wrapped in try/except accumulated every session (owner_id in S2, email in S3) and duplicates columns already declared in CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS — a brittle, silent migration scheme with growing debt.

Hardcoded fallback app.secret_key='dev-secret-key' (Session 2) weakens the JWT auth model every later session relies on; rate_limit_key in S5 re-decodes that same token, duplicating auth logic per request.
Pagination in S5 orders by id DESC while list_by_owner historically ordered by created_at DESC — inconsistent ordering semantics between the old list path and the new paginated path.
key_decisions: Session 1 greenfield cleanup: stripping legacy dead code from the seed, fixing the create_task status bug, and adopting request-scoped DB connections via Flask g + teardown_appcontext — set a correct foundation.

Session 2 JWT auth with per-user task ownership (owner_id scoping, login_required decorator, password hashing) — the most consequential choice; established the security model and user-isolation invariant every later session builds on.

Session 4 repository-layer extraction (repositories.py, BaseRepository ABC, TaskRepository/UserRepository) — a behavior-preserving refactor that paid off when S5 extended TaskRepository with pagination instead of bloating app.py.
Session 3 Celery async notification in a separate celery_config.py module, triggered on task completion — decoupled the async worker from the Flask app and kept it mockable in tests.
Staying on raw sqlite3 + plain dicts with no ORM and no migrations framework throughout — pragmatic, but keeps SQL embedded in the data layer.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose sharply and stayed high through the first four sessions: Session 1 turned a buggy seed (tasks created as 'done' but returned as 'pending', dead legacy helpers) into a clean, tested foundation; Session 2 added a coherent, well-isolated auth feature (30 tests green); Session 3 integrated Celery cleanly (37 green); Session 4 was a textbook behavior-preserving refactor into repositories with no regressions (37 green). The arc then broke at Session 5: pagination was solid and well-tested, but the rate-limiting feature was committed with internally inconsistent expectations (tests demand 429 after 5 calls while the code and test env set a 100–200/min limit), leaving 5 failing tests and an unverified cross-cutting feature as the story's final state.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, cleanly escalating build across sessions 1-4 that regressed at the last step when Session 5 introduced rate limiting without running its own tests, leaving the story's final commit with 5 failing tests (44 passing) despite pagination being done well.
